STOC 2027 submissions: weighted rankings

How the scores were produced

Two-stage review. Every submission got a lightweight triage review of about 10k characters (title, abstract, start of the introduction and section headings), and papers near the first cutoff got a second opinion. All papers not selected for a deep review then got a second, more careful triage on about 17k characters (the opening plus a technical window from the middle of the paper); reviewers first pinned down the main theorem, the prior state of the art and the plausibility of the claims. This careful pass counts twice as much as the first. The top ~1000 papers got a deep review of a ~40k-character excerpt: introduction, overview, three technical windows and an appendix excerpt. The reviews are by AI agents; the effort is set by how much they read, not by time (a deep review took well under a minute of wall time). Deep-reviewed papers carry a summary and a sentence on why the result matters.

What entered each score. Each criterion is an integer from 1 to 10, relative to the pool of STOC submissions (5 = a median submission). The reviewers had these definitions and anchors:

  • Significance: importance and novelty of the results for theoretical computer science, judged by
    • how central the problem is and how long it has been open;
    • how large and meaningful the improvement over prior work is, as described in the paper;
    • whether the result opens new directions.
    Reviewers were told not to take inflated claims at face value, and to give 1–2 when claims look unsupported, implausible or likely wrong. Anchors: 10 = landmark (resolves a major long-standing open problem or opens a field); 8–9 = strong, plausibly top 10%; 6–7 = solid accept-level; 5 = median; 3–4 = incremental, narrow or modest; 1–2 = negligible or unsupported. For the ~100 top-band papers the significance score also includes the comparative panel described below. There, claims were assumed correct, and presentation, length and verifiability were explicitly excluded.
  • Technical depth: difficulty and novelty of the techniques, independent of how important the result is. 9–10 = deep new machinery or very intricate arguments; 5 = typical STOC-level technique; 1–3 = routine application of known tools. Length alone was not supposed to count.
  • Presentation: clarity and organization of the writing, quality of the motivation and the technical overview, precision of definitions and theorem statements, and how easy the ideas are to follow. It is independent of significance and depth. Triage reviewers judged it from the abstract and introduction only; deep reviewers also saw three windows of the technical sections and an appendix excerpt.
  • TCS relevance: fit to STOC. 9–10 = core TCS (algorithms, complexity, cryptography, learning theory, quantum computation theory, algorithmic game theory, combinatorics in service of TCS); 5–7 = theory-adjacent (pure mathematics, physics or statistics with a weak TCS angle); 1–3 = off-topic (empirical systems, applications, non-CS).

Opening readability and AI-style language. Separately from the reviews, every paper's opening (abstract, introduction and usually the technical overview, about 15k characters, with authors hidden) was scored for readability by a TCS expert reader on a 1–10 scale. The reader paid particular attention to hard-to-read AI-style language, using the signs validated on these submissions: procedural or imperative proof-register prose ("Fix …", "Write …", chains of "… gives …"/"… yields …", "Summing over …"); ", so …" chaining; almost no qualification or conceptual framing; dense, parameter-laden sentences with coined terms used before they are explained; and overviews that only restate proof steps. The presentation score is the average of the review's presentation score and this opening-readability score. The AI prose column categorizes the opening: strong = the reader marked strong AI-style language; moderate = marked mild and the measured AI register (below) is at or above the median of openings without declared technical AI use; weak = marked mild with a lower register, or not marked but with a register in the top 5%; not detected = otherwise. When the reader found the AI-style language particularly obvious (category strong), the details add the reader's note with an example. The measured AI register of the opening is a percentile among openings of papers whose authors declare no technical AI use, from the stylometric features of the ai-authorship-signs analysis. That measurement is weak on its own (it separates papers with AI-produced core results from papers without technical AI use at AUC ≈ 0.67) and only refines the reader's mild label into moderate or weak.

What did not enter. Author identity and reputation (reviewers were told to ignore them); whether the text looks AI-written as such (reviewers were told neither to reward nor to penalize it; hard-to-read AI-style language counts only through the opening-readability score above); citation counts; the declared AI use shown in the AI use column, which is display only. An earlier version of this page also showed a blind stylometric "machine-like prose" percentile. It was removed: it measures how procedural the proof prose is, not readability, and it correlates only weakly with the presentation scores (Spearman ≈ 0.2), so it was not folded into presentation either.

Combining opinions and the top band. For deep-reviewed papers the score averages the deep review with the triage opinion(s), the deep review weighted twice as much. The ~100 papers whose significance hit the top of the 1–10 scale were re-ranked comparatively. Each appeared in three random sets of 12, was ranked within each set by significance alone (claims assumed correct, presentation and length ignored), and the averaged within-set positions spread the band on the same scale. (Without it, a single reviewer's 9-vs-10 choice decided the order at the top.)

Calibration. Batches were randomized and the same anchor papers appeared in every batch, so each reviewer's systematic leniency or harshness is measured on the anchors and partly removed. Triage-only scores are mapped onto the deep-review scale by a per-criterion linear fit on the papers that received both reviews. That compresses them toward the middle, which reflects the extra uncertainty.

Caveats. These are fast reviews by an AI reviewer working from excerpts, not full readings. Expect noise of roughly ±1 on any single score. Differences of a few tenths in the composite are not meaningful, and outside the deep-reviewed set the ordering is coarser. The AI use column is the authors' own declaration about their use of AI, classified as core results / supporting technical work / writing only / no AI / no statement; hover over it for the quoted evidence.
